planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Little Moonshine is a compact sport of the classic Moonshine yarrow, staying under a foot tall.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; rich or overly wet soil causes weak, floppy growth in this compact cultivar. Little Moonshine is a dwarf selection of the popular Moonshine yarrow, holding the same clear sulfur-yellow, flat-topped flower clusters above silvery, finely dissected, aromatic foliage, but staying under a foot tall and rarely needing staking. It blooms from early summer through fall, especially with regular deadheading, and is a strong draw for butterflies and other pollinators while resisting deer and rabbits. Its low, dense habit suits rock gardens, border fronts, and containers where the taller Moonshine would overwhelm the scale. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: The Pearl Sneezewort (Double White Pompon Yarrow)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or plant divisions in spring, into moist, average to fertile soil in full sun to light shade; The Pearl tolerates more moisture than most yarrows.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; unlike the drought-loving Achillea millefolium types, this sneezewort selection tolerates and even prefers more consistent moisture, including damp border edges and pond margins. The Pearl produces masses of small, fully double, button-like white flowers resembling tiny pompons or pearls, held on wiry branching stems above narrow, toothed, deep-green foliage from midsummer into early fall, and is a long-standing favorite for cutting and for lightening dark-flowered summer borders. It can spread by rhizomes into loose colonies over time, so divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep it in bounds and vigorous. Stake in windy or overly rich sites, since the fluffy flower heads can become top-heavy.

common_name: New Vintage Red Yarrow (Compact Non-Fading Red Yarrow)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; New Vintage Red stays compact and well-branched without pinching.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage prevents the crown rot that troubles yarrow in heavy, wet ground. New Vintage Red is a compact, heavily branched selection bred for garden performance, bearing flat-topped clusters of deep crimson-red flowers with cream centers that hold their rich color through the season instead of fading to tan or brown like many older red yarrows. It flowers continuously from early summer to early fall above ferny, aromatic gray-green foliage, with no gap between the foliage mound and the bloom stems, and its dense, tidy habit suits border fronts and containers without staking. Deadhead spent clusters to prolong bloom, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: New Vintage White Yarrow (Compact Non-Fading White Yarrow)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; New Vintage White is a compact, sturdy grower that rarely needs staking.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; rich, wet soil leads to floppy, weak-stemmed growth in this drought-tough selection. New Vintage White is a compact, densely branched yarrow cultivar producing pure white, flat-topped flower clusters with creamy centers continuously from early summer into early fall, held tightly above finely cut, aromatic gray-green foliage with no gap between the flowers and the leaf mound. Its short, well-branched habit makes it useful for border fronts, mixed containers, and xeriscape plantings where taller yarrows would need staking. Deadhead through the season to sustain bloom and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Grape Sensation Blanket Flower (Purple-Pink Texas Firewheel)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in very well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to bright part shade; Grape Sensation forms an airy clump that is very long-lived once established.

directions: Plant in very well-drained to dry, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to bright part shade; never plant in rich, moist ground, which shortens the life of this Texas native selection. Grape Sensation is a selected form of the wild Texas firewheel (Gaillardia aestivalis var. winkleri) prized for its unusual hot-pink-to-purple ray petals with a dark burgundy central disk, a striking departure from the typical red-and-yellow blanket flower color scheme, borne on wiry, airy stems from mid-spring through fall without deadheading. It is exceptionally long-lived and heat-tolerant for a gaillardia, thriving in the lean, dry, sandy soils of its East Texas pineland origin, and even its spent flower heads keep their dark color, so the plant remains attractive as it goes to seed. Bees and butterflies visit the blooms heavily; divide only occasionally, since this selection resents disturbance once established.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Miss Willmott Caucasian Pincushion Flower (White Scabiosa)

planting.note: Plant divisions around last frost into alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; this heirloom white selection has been grown since the early 20th century and is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit holder.

directions: Plant in fertile, alkaline to neutral, sharply drained soil in full sun, since this old cultivar declines quickly in acidic or heavy wet ground. Miss Willmott is one of the classic named Scabiosa caucasica selections, bearing creamy-white, 2-3 inch pincushion flowers with a domed center of tightly packed disc florets ringed by ruffled outer petals, held on long wiry stems that make it outstanding for cutting. Named in honor of the celebrated Edwardian horticulturist Ellen Willmott, it has been grown in cottage and cutting gardens for over a century and pairs beautifully with the lavender-blue 'Clive Greaves' selection. Deadhead continuously through the season to sustain bloom from midsummer into fall, and divide clumps every three to four years since crowded crowns lose vigor. Good air circulation helps prevent powdery mildew in humid climates.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring, or start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, into lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; self-sows readily once established.

directions: Direct sow, or plant divisions, in lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rich, moist soil produces floppy, short-lived plants. Cream pincushion flower is a European and western Asian native species bearing airy, wiry-stemmed clumps topped with abundant small, creamy-yellow pincushion flower heads from early summer to frost, a softer and less commonly grown color than the lavender-blue or crimson scabious more typically planted. Its fine texture and pastel color make it an excellent filler among stronger-colored perennials, and the long, slender stems bob and sway in the slightest breeze, drawing a steady stream of bees, hoverflies, and butterflies. It is more drought-tolerant and lean-soil-adapted than Scabiosa caucasica, thriving in the same conditions favored by lavender and other Mediterranean-style plantings, and self-sows modestly to naturalize a colony over time.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Flutter Deep Blue is compact and free-flowering without deadheading.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; consistently soggy soil shortens the life of this compact selection. Flutter Deep Blue is a basal-clumping pincushion flower cultivar bred for a long, heavy bloom season, producing large, lilac-blue, button-like flowers on upright stems above mounds of lacy, gray-green, fuzzy foliage from early spring through the first hard frost with minimal deadheading required. Its tidy, compact habit suits border fronts, containers, and cutting gardens alike, and the abundant nectar-rich blooms are a strong draw for bees and butterflies throughout the season. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor, and ensure sharp drainage, since the crown is prone to rot in heavy or poorly drained soils.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring; field scabious establishes best in lean, unamended soil typical of meadow and wildflower plantings and can also be started indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost.

directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun, or lightly rake seed into an existing meadow or wildflower planting; field scabious is a widespread European native perennial of unimproved grasslands and calcareous meadows that has become a staple of pollinator seed mixes. It produces branching, wiry stems topped with lavender-blue to lilac pincushion flowers from June through September, each head made up of a domed center of disc florets ringed by larger, ragged-edged outer florets, and is one of the most heavily visited late-summer nectar sources for bees, hoverflies, and butterflies in its native range. Unlike the more compact garden Knautia macedonica, field scabious tolerates lean, unimproved soil and mowing after seed set, making it well suited to naturalistic meadow plantings rather than formal borders. It is a biennial to short-lived perennial that self-sows readily to maintain a permanent colony once established.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring after the danger of hard frost has passed, into lean, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; Pretty Betsy also self-sows readily where happy.

directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; rich or waterlogged soil produces weak, sprawling growth. Pretty Betsy is a quick-growing annual cousin of the shrubby red valerian (Centranthus ruber), native to Spain and North Africa, forming low, bushy plants covered from late spring through summer in small, spurred, pink-to-rose flowers with a paler throat, clustered at the stem tips. It is easy from seed, blooms within weeks of sowing, and tolerates poor, dry, rocky soil that would stunt many other annuals, making it a good fit for gravel gardens, border edges, and containers. Deadhead lightly to prolong bloom, or allow some flowers to set seed for reliable self-sowing the following year. Its nectar-rich flowers attract bees and butterflies throughout its bloom period.
